entries.038f9dd5ea75d355c1d6b39343b31bc87b558370: <div sID="gen12006" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="85" osisID="Ps.85" sID="Ps.85"/> <div eID="gen12006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12007" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12008" type="x-p"/> Interpreters are generally of the opinion that this psalm was penned after the return of the Jews out of their captivity in Babylon, when they still remained under some tokens of God's displeasure, which they here pray for the removal of. And nothing appears to the contrary, but that it might be penned then, as well as <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9">Ps. cxxxvii.</reference> They are the public interests that lie near the psalmist's heart here, and the psalm is penned for the great congregation. The church was here in a deluge; above were clouds, below were waves; every thing was dark and dismal. The church is like Noah in the ark, between life and death, between hope and fear; being so, I. Here is the dove sent forth in prayer. The petitions are against sin and wrath (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.4">ver. 4</reference>) and for mercy and grace, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">ver. 7</reference>. The pleas are taken from former favours (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.3">ver. 1-3</reference>) and present distresses, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.5-Ps.85.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. II. Here is the dove returning with an olive branch of peace and good tidings; the psalmist expects her return (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">ver. 8</reference>) and then recounts the favours to God's Israel which by the spirit of prophecy he gave assurance of to others, and by the spirit of faith he took the assurance of to himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9-Ps.85.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. In singing this psalm we may be assisted in our prayers to God both for his church in general and for the land of our nativity in particular. The former part will be of use to direct our desires, the latter to encourage our faith and hope in those prayers.
entries.4a5f14c4e71831cb839ee26047316491bbb2fc5c: <div eID="gen12008" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12007" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer in Time of Trouble.</title> <div sID="gen12009" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou hast taken away all thy wrath: thou hast turned <hi type="italic">thyself</hi> from the fierceness of thine anger. <hi type="super">4</hi> Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease. <hi type="super">5</hi> Wilt thou be angry with us for ever? wilt thou draw out thine anger to all generations? <hi type="super">6</hi> Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee? <hi type="super">7</hi> show us thy mercy, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and grant us thy salvation. <div eID="gen12009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12010" type="x-p"/> The church, in affliction and distress, is here, by direction from God, making her application to God. So ready is God to hear and answer the prayers of his people that by his Spirit in the word, and in the heart, he indites their petitions and puts words into their mouths. The people of God, in a very low and weak condition, are here taught how to address themselves to God. <div eID="gen12010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12011" type="x-p"/> I. They are to acknowledge with thankfulness the great things God had done for them (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.3">v. 1-3</reference>): "Thou has done so and so for us and our fathers." Note, The sense of present afflictions should not drown the remembrance of former mercies; but, even when we are brought very low, we must call to remembrance past experiences of God's goodness, which we must take notice of with thankfulness, to his praise. They speak of it here with pleasure, 1. That God had shown himself propitious to their land, and had smiled upon it as his own: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast been favourable to thy land,</hi> as thine, with distinguishing favours." Note, The favour of God is the spring-head of all good, and the fountain of happiness, to nations, as well as to particular persons. It was by the favour of God that Israel got and kept possession of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Ps. xliv. 3</reference>); and, if he had not continued very favourable to them, they would have been ruined many a time. 2. That he had rescued them out of the hands of their enemies and restored them to their liberty: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob,</hi> and settled those in their own land again that had been driven out and were strangers in a strange land, prisoners in the land of their oppressors." The captivity of Jacob, though it may continue long, will be brought back in due time. 3. That he had not dealt with them according to the desert of their provocations (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people,</hi> and not punished them as in justice thou mightest. <hi type="italic">Thou hast covered all their sin.</hi>" When God forgives sin he covers it; and, when he covers the sin of his people, he covers it all. The bringing back of their captivity was <hi type="italic">then</hi> an instance of God's favour to them, when it was accompanied with the pardon of their iniquity. 4. That he had not continued his anger against them so far, and so long, as they had reason to fear (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.3">v. 3</reference>): "Having <hi type="italic">covered all their sin,</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">taken away all thy wrath;</hi>" for when sin is set aside God's anger ceases; God is pacified if we are purified. See what the pardon of sin is: <hi type="italic">Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people,</hi> that is, "<hi type="italic">Thou hast turned thy anger from waxing hot,</hi> so as to consume us in the flame of it. In compassion to us thou hast not stirred up all thy wrath, but, when an intercessor has stood before thee in the gap, thou hast turned away thy anger." <div eID="gen12011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12012" type="x-p"/> II. They are taught to pray to God for grace and mercy, in reference to their present distress; this is inferred from the former: "Thou hast done well for our fathers; do well for us, for we are the children of the same covenant." 1. They pray for converting grace: "<hi type="italic">Turn us, O God of our salvation!</hi> in order to the turning of our captivity; turn us from iniquity; turn us to thyself and to our duty; turn us, and we shall be turned." All those whom God will save sooner or later he will turn. If no conversion, no salvation. 2. They pray for the removal of the tokens of God's displeasure which they were under: "<hi type="italic">Cause thine anger towards us to cease,</hi> as thou didst many a time cause it to cease in the days of our fathers, when thou didst take away thy wrath from them." Observe the method, "First turn us to thee, and then cause thy anger to turn from us." When we are reconciled to God, then, and not till then, we may expect the comfort of his being reconciled to us. 3. They pray for the manifestation of God's good-will to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Show us thy mercy, O Lord!</hi> show thyself merciful to us; not only have mercy on us, but let us have the comfortable evidences of that mercy; let us know that thou hast mercy on us and mercy in store for us." 4. They pray that God would, graciously to them and gloriously to himself, appear on their behalf: "<hi type="italic">Grant us thy salvation;</hi> grant it by thy promise, and then, no doubt, thou wilt work it by thy providence." Note, The vessels of God's mercy are the heirs of his salvation; he shows mercy to those to whom he grants salvation; for salvation is of mere mercy. <div eID="gen12012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12013" type="x-p"/> III. They are taught humbly to expostulate with God concerning their present troubles, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.5-Ps.85.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Here observe, 1. What they dread and deprecate: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou be angry with us for ever?</hi> We are undone if thou art, but we hope thou wilt not. <hi type="italic">Wilt thou draw out thy anger unto all generations?</hi> No; thou art gracious, slow to anger, and swift to show mercy, and wilt not contend for ever. Thou wast not angry with our fathers for ever, but didst soon turn thyself from the fierceness of thy wrath; why then wilt thou be angry with us for ever? Are not thy mercies and compassions as plentiful and powerful as ever they were? Impenitent sinners God will be angry with for ever; for what is hell but the wrath of God drawn out unto endless generations? But shall a hell upon earth be the lot of thy people?" 2. What they desire and hope for: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou not revive us again</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.6">v. 6</reference>), revive us with comforts spoken to us, revive us with deliverances wrought for us? Thou hast been favourable to thy land formerly, and that revived it; wilt thou not again be favourable, and so revive it again?" God had granted to the children of the captivity <hi type="italic">some reviving in their bondage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>. Their return out of Babylon was as <hi type="italic">life from the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.11-Ezek.37.12">Eze. xxxvii. 11, 12</reference>. Now, Lord (say they), <hi type="italic">wilt thou not revive us again,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put thy hand again the second time</hi> to gather us in? <reference osisRef="Isa.126.1 Isa.126.4 Ps.126.1 Ps.126.4">Ps. cxxvi. 1, 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Revive thy work in the midst of the years,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Hab. iii. 2</reference>. "Revive us again," (1.) "That thy people may rejoice; and so we shall have the comfort of it," <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Ps. xiv. 7</reference>. Give them life, that they may have joy. (2.) "That they may rejoice in thee; and so thou wilt have the glory of it." If God be the fountain of all our mercies, he must be the centre of all our joys.
entries.c2e48ab63ed298f96fed9aa74f5ee8f31407d659: <div eID="gen12013" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Answer to Prayer; Blessings Given in Answer to Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen12014" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> I will hear what God the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly. <hi type="super">9</hi> Surely his salvation <hi type="italic">is</hi> nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land. <hi type="super">10</hi> Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed <hi type="italic">each other.</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven. <hi type="super">12</hi> Yea, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall give <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> good; and our land shall yield her increase. <hi type="super">13</hi> Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set <hi type="italic">us</hi> in the way of his steps. <div eID="gen12014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12015" type="x-p"/> We have here an answer to the prayers and expostulations in the <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.7">foregoing verses</reference>. <div eID="gen12015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12016" type="x-p"/> I. In general, it is an answer of peace. This the psalmist is soon aware of (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">v. 8</reference>), for he <hi type="italic">stands upon his watch-tower</hi> to <hi type="italic">hear what God will say unto him,</hi> as the prophet, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1-Hab.2.2">Hab. ii. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will hear what God the Lord will speak.</hi> This intimates, 1. The stilling of his passions—his grief, his fear—and the tumult of his spirit which they occasioned: "Compose thyself, O my soul! in a humble silence to attend upon God and wait his motions. I have spoken enough, or too much; now I will hear what God will speak, and welcome his holy will. <hi type="italic">What saith my Lord unto his servant?</hi>" If we would have God to hear what we say to him by prayer, we must be ready to hear what he says to us by his word. 2. The raising of his expectation; now that he has been at prayer he looks for something very great, and very kind, from the God that hears prayer. When we have prayed we should look after our prayers, and stay for an answer. Now observe here, (1.) What it is that he promises himself from God, in answer to his prayers: <hi type="italic">He will speak peace to his people, and to his saints.</hi> There are a people in the world who are God's people, set apart for him, subject to him, and who shall be saved by him. All his people are his saints, sanctified by his grace and devoted to his glory; these may sometimes want peace, when without are fightings and within are fears; but, sooner or later, God will speak peace to them; if he do not command outward peace, yet he will suggest inward peace, speaking that to their hearts by his Spirit which he has spoken to their ears by his word and ministers and making them to hear joy and gladness. (2.) What use he makes of this expectation. [1.] He takes the comfort of it; and so must we: "<hi type="italic">I will hear what God the Lord will speak,</hi> hear the assurances he gives of peace, in answer to prayer." When God speaks peace we must not be deaf to it, but with all humility and thankfulness receive it. [2.] He cautions the saints to do the duty which this calls for: <hi type="italic">But let them not turn again to folly;</hi> for it is on these terms, and no other, that peace is to be expected. To those, and those only, peace is spoken, who turn from sin; but, if they return to it again, it is at their peril. All sin is folly, but especially backsliding; it is egregious folly to turn to sin after we have seemed to turn from it, to turn to it after God has spoken peace. God is for peace, but, when he speaks, such are for war. <div eID="gen12016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12017" type="x-p"/> II. Here are the particulars of this answer of peace. He doubts not but all will be well in a little time, and therefore gives us the pleasing prospect of the flourishing estate of the church in the <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9-Ps.85.13">last five verses</reference> of the psalm, which describe the peace and prosperity that God, at length, blessed the children of the captivity with, when, after a great deal of toil and agitation, at length they gained a settlement in their own land. But it may be taken both as a promise also to all who fear God and work righteousness, that they shall be easy and happy, and as a prophecy of the kingdom of the Messiah and the blessings with which that kingdom should be enriched. Here is, <div eID="gen12017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12018" type="x-p"/> 1. Help at hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Surely his salvation is nigh,</hi> nigh to us, nigher than we think it is: it will soon be effected, how great soever our difficulties and distresses are, when God's time shall come, and that time is not far off." When the tale of bricks is doubled, then Moses comes. It is nigh to all who fear him; when trouble is nigh salvation is nigh, for God is a very present help in time of trouble to all who are his; whereas <hi type="italic">salvation is far from the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.155">Ps. cxix. 155</reference>. This may fitly be applied to Christ the author of eternal salvation: it was the comfort of the Old-Testament saints that, though they lived not to see that redemption in Jerusalem which they waited for, yet they were sure it was nigh, and would be welcome, to all that fear God. <div eID="gen12018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> 2. Honour secured: "<hi type="italic">That glory may dwell in our land,</hi> that we may have the worship of God settled and established among us; for that is the glory of a land. When that goes, <hi type="italic">Ichabod—the glory has departed;</hi> when that stays glory dwells." This may refer to the Messiah, who was to be <hi type="italic">the glory of his people Israel,</hi> and who came and dwelt among them (<reference osisRef="John.1.4">John i. 4</reference>), for which reason their land is called <hi type="italic">Immanuel's land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Isa. viii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> 3. Graces meeting, and happily embracing (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.10-Ps.85.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Mercy and truth, righteousness and peace, kiss each other.</hi> This may be understood, (1.) Of the reformation of the people and of the government, in the administration of which all those graces should be conspicuous and commanding. The rulers and ruled shall all be merciful and true, righteous and peaceable. When there is no truth nor mercy all goes to ruin (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.1">Hos. iv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.14-Isa.59.15">Isa. lix. 14, 15</reference>); but when these meet in the management of all affairs, when these give aim, when these give law, when there is such plenty of truth that it sprouts up like the grass of the earth, and of righteousness that it is showered down like rain from heaven, then things go well. When in every congress mercy and truth meet, in every embrace righteousness and peace kiss, and common honesty is indeed common, then glory dwells in a land, as the sin of reigning dishonesty is a reproach to any people. (2.) Of the return of God's favour, and the continuance of it, thereupon. When a people return to God and adhere to him in a way of duty he will return to them and abide with them in a way of mercy. So some understand this, man's truth and God's mercy, man's righteousness and God's peace, meet together. If God find us true to him, to one another, to ourselves, we shall find him merciful. If we make conscience of righteousness, we shall have the comfort of peace. If <hi type="italic">truth spring out of the earth,</hi> that is (as Dr. Hammond expounds it), out of the hearts of men, the proper soil for it to grow in, righteousness (that is, God's mercy) shall look down from heaven, as the sun does upon the world when it sheds its influences on the productions of the earth and cherishes them. (3.) Of the harmony of the divine attributes in the Messiah's undertaking. In him who is both our salvation and our glory <hi type="italic">mercy and truth have met together;</hi> God's mercy and truth, and his <hi type="italic">righteousness and peace, have kissed each other;</hi> that is, the great affair of our salvation is so well contrived, so well concerted, that God may have mercy upon poor sinners, and be at peace with them, without any wrong to his truth and righteousness. He is true to the threatening, and just in his government, and yet pardons sinners and takes them into covenant with himself. Christ, as Mediator, brings heaven and earth together again, which sin had set at variance; through him <hi type="italic">truth springs out of the earth,</hi> that truth which God <hi type="italic">desires in the inward part,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">righteousness looks down from heaven;</hi> for God is <hi type="italic">just, and the justifier of those who believe in Jesus.</hi> Or it may denote that in the kingdom of the Messiah these graces shall flourish and prevail and have a universal command. <div eID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12021" type="x-p"/> 4. Great plenty of every thing desirable (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall give that which is good,</hi> every thing that he sees to be good for us. All good comes from God's goodness; and when mercy, truth, and righteousness, have a sovereign influence on men's hearts and lives, all good may be expected. If we thus <hi type="italic">seek the righteousness of God's kingdom, other things shall be added;</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Matt. vi. 33</reference>. When the glory of the gospel dwells in our land, then it shall yield its increase, for soul-prosperity will either bring outward prosperity along with it or sweeten the want of it. See <reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">Ps. lxvii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen12021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12022" type="x-p"/> 5. A sure guidance in the good way (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">The righteousness</hi> of his promise which he has made to us, assuring us of happiness, and the righteousness of sanctification, that good work which he has wrought in us, these shall go before him to prepare his way, both to raise our expectations of his favour and to qualify us for it; and these shall go before us also, and be our guide to <hi type="italic">set us in the way of his steps,</hi> that is, to encourage our hopes and guide our practice, that we may go forth to meet him when he is coming towards us in ways of mercy. Christ, the sun of righteousness, shall bring us to God, and put us into the way that leads to him. John Baptist, a preacher of righteousness, shall go before Christ to prepare his way. Righteousness is a sure guide both in meeting God and in following him.  <chapter eID="Ps.85"/> <div eID="gen12022" type="x-p"/>

They are here termed "them that fear him"; and grace produces glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Psa 84:11</reference>). <div eID="gen9947" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccd41413436b0f50a600ab6135dc2dfccc0aba03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6491"/><div sID="gen9948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6491"/>10. God's promises of "mercy" will be verified by His "truth" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">Psa 25:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">40:10</reference>); and the "work of righteousness" in His holy government shall be "peace" (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Is 32:17</reference>). There is an implied contrast with a dispensation under which God's truth sustains His threatened wrath, and His righteousness inflicts misery on the wicked. <div eID="gen9948" type="x-p"/>

entries.5ea8c57e4b7ba9aa83f66f0cc0b08b4143d0d5b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6493"/><div sID="gen9950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6493"/>12-13. and, under this, the deserted land shall be productive, and men be "set," or guided in God's holy ways. Doubtless, in this description of God's returning favor, the writer had in view that more glorious period, when Christ shall establish His government on God's reconciled justice and abounding mercy. <chapter eID="Ps.85"/>

entries.a63753f35f64511b21038446c6728e8d1d15af88: <div eID="gen21349" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21350" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21351" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21351" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21350" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21352" type="x-p"/> Thanksgiving to God for restoration to the Divine favor, <reference osisRef="Psa.85.1-Psa.85.3">Psa 85:1-3</reference>; prayer for farther mercies, <reference osisRef="Psa.85.4-Psa.85.7">Psa 85:4-7</reference>; the psalmist waits for a gracious answer in full confidence of receiving it, <reference osisRef="Psa.85.8">Psa 85:8</reference>. He receives the assurance of the greatest blessings, and exults in the prospect, <reference osisRef="Psa.85.9-Psa.85.13">Psa 85:9-13</reference>. <div eID="gen21352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21353" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm we have seen before, <reference osisRef="Psa.42.1-Psa.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference> : As to the time, it seems to have been written during, or even after, the return from the Babylonish captivity. In the three first verses the psalmist acknowledges the goodness of God in bringing the people back to their own land; he next prays to God to restore them to their ancient prosperity. In the spirit of prophecy, he waits on God, and hears him promise to do it; and then exults in the prospect of so great a good. The whole Psalm seems also to have a reference to the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen21353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21354" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21355" type="x-p"/> Lord, thou hast been favorable - Literally, Thou hast been well pleased with thy land. <div eID="gen21355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21356" type="x-p"/> Thou hast brought back the captivity - This seems to fix the time of the Psalm to be after the return of the Jews from Babylon.
entries.29a78ae2ae09fc5c89a18ded1aeaacea41ee1d4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21357" type="x-p"/> Thou hast forgiven the iniquity - נשאת עון nasatha avon, Thou hast borne, or carried away, the iniquity. An allusion to the ceremony of the scapegoat. <div eID="gen21357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21358" type="x-p"/> Thou hast covered all their sin - As thou hast freely forgiven it, its offensiveness and abominable nature no longer appear. The whole is put out of sight; and, as we are restored from our captivity, the consequences no longer appear. <div eID="gen21358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21359" type="x-p"/> Selah - This is true. Our return to our own land is the full proof.
entries.3a75d4fbcd4d09aa5cde781472719857b3d6eba4: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21360" type="x-p"/> Thou hast taken away - אספת asaphta, "Thou hast gathered up all thy wrath." This carries on the metaphor in the second verse: "Thou hast collected all thy wrath, and carried it away with all our iniquities."
entries.73bb622e4ab17f62bbbb2ad496cebf2def28fb9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21361" type="x-p"/> Turn us, O God of our salvation - Thou hast turned our captivity; now convert our souls. And they find a reason for their prayer in an attribute of their God; the God of their salvation. And as his work was to save, they beg that his anger towards them might cease. The Israelites were not restored from their captivity all at once. A few returned with Zerubbabel; some more with Ezra and Nehemiah; but a great number still remained in Babylonia, Media, Assyria, Egypt, and other parts. The request of the psalmist is, to have a complete restoration of all the Israelites from all places of their dispersion.
entries.23f34e5c2d3521098b20017fb3952be4905bf333: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21362" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou draw out thine anger - We have already suffered much and long; our fathers have suffered, and we have succeeded to their distresses. Draw not out thy anger against us from generation to generation.
entries.9949a1b53043264ede814b1d592bfef570419b59: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21363" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou not revive us - We have long had the sentence of death in ourselves; and have feared an utter extinction. Shall not our nation yet live before thee? Shall we not become once more numerous, pious, and powerful, that <div eID="gen21363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21364" type="x-p"/> Thy people may rejoice in thee? - As the Source of all our mercies; and give thee the glory due to thy name?
entries.b49bdec004f4d93a4bc2baf8d28809f9cb0b1817: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21365" type="x-p"/> Show us thy mercy - Blot out all our sins. <div eID="gen21365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21366" type="x-p"/> And grant us thy salvation - Give us such a complete deliverance as is worthy of thy majesty and mercy to bestow!
entries.a3827f08b687edcefdd40ed1fe865db767508dc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21367" type="x-p"/> I will hear what God the Lord will speak - The psalmist goes as a prophet to consult the Lord; and, having made his request, waits an answer from the spirit of prophecy. He is satisfied that the answer will be gracious; and having received it he relates it to the people. <div eID="gen21367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21368" type="x-p"/> He will speak peace - He will give prosperity to the people in general; and to his saints - his followers, in particular. <div eID="gen21368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21369" type="x-p"/> But let them not turn again to folly - Let them not abuse the mercy of their God, by sinning any more against him.
entries.0ca9e95442cde887531c1bd60e5d4fe35ecea059: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21370" type="x-p"/> Surely his salvation is nigh - To him who fears God, and trembles at his word, his salvation is nigh at hand. <div eID="gen21370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21371" type="x-p"/> That glory may dwell in our land - That thy worship may be restored, the temple rebuilt, and the Divine shechinah, or symbol of the presence of God, resume its place. The pure and undefiled religion of God preached, professed, and experienced in a nation, is the glory of that land. The Prophet Haggai had said that the glory of the latter house - the temple built after their return from Babylon, should be greater than the glory of the former, viz., of that built by Solomon: but, as a building, it was far inferior to the former; yet it had a superior glory in being visited by Jesus Christ. This was the glory that excelled.
entries.40c04281d8cc0f42adb681bb49235b8e0719367d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21372" type="x-p"/> Mercy and truth are met together - It would be more simple to translate the original: - חסד ואמת נפגשו צדק ושלום נשקו <div eID="gen21372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21373" type="x-p"/> Chesed veemeth niphgashu; <div eID="gen21373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21374" type="x-p"/> Tsedek veshalom nashaku, - " <div eID="gen21374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21375" type="x-p"/> Mercy and truth have met on the way <div eID="gen21375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21376" type="x-p"/> Righteousness and peace have embraced." <div eID="gen21376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21377" type="x-p"/> This is a remarkable text, and much has been said on it: but there is a beauty in it which, I think, has not been noticed. <div eID="gen21377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21378" type="x-p"/> Mercy and peace are on one side; truth and righteousness on the other. Truth requires righteousness; mercy calls for peace. <div eID="gen21378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21379" type="x-p"/> They meet together on the way; one going to make inquisition for sin, the other to plead for reconciliation. Having met, their differences on certain considerations, not here particularly mentioned are adjusted; and their mutual claims are blended together in one common interest; on which peace and righteousness immediately embrace. Thus, righteousness is given to truth, and peace is given to mercy. <div eID="gen21379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21380" type="x-p"/> Now, Where did these meet? In Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen21380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21381" type="x-p"/> When were they reconciled? When he poured out his life on Calvary.
entries.392ae7c00158ac55076468552ee6bba828b2acb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21382" type="x-p"/> Truth shall spring out of the earth - In consequence of this wonderful reconciliation, the truth of God shall prevail among men. The seeds of it shall be so plentifully sown by the preaching of Christ and his apostles that true religion shall be diffused over the world. <div eID="gen21382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21383" type="x-p"/> And righteousness shall look down from heaven - And be delighted with the reformation of the sons of Adam; and shall be so satisfled with the glorious work which is carried forward, that,
entries.01d5f0138db87711cddd5cfe4fb28910f4ba21bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21384" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall give - good - הטוב hattob, The Good thing - what is the supreme good, the summum bonum, for which man has searched in vain through all his generations. Those who are reconciled to him through the Son of his love shall enjoy the favor of their God; to have which is the supreme happiness of man. <div eID="gen21384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21385" type="x-p"/> Our land shall yield her increase - There shall be neither dearth nor barrenness; for truth, that springs out of the earth, shall yield an abundant harvest, in the conversion of all nations to the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ.
entries.630208a27a1f5363b82bb110ada121027de4db99: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21386" type="x-p"/> Righteousness shall go before him - Perhaps this verse may receive its best solution from <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Rom 3:25</reference> : "Whom God hath set for a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his Righteousness for the remission of sins that are past." This term the apostle uses to point out God's method of justifying or saving mankind. And this, in the preaching of the pure Gospel, is ever going before to point out the Lord Jesus, and the redemption that is in his blood. And thus going before him, the sinner, who feels his need of salvation, is Set - in the way of his steps; as Bartimeus sat by the way-side begging, by which way Jesus walked; and when he came where he was, heard his prayer, and restored him his sight. Or, righteousness - the pure and holy law of God, must be proclaimed as broken by sinners, and calling aloud for vengeance, before they can see and feel their need of Christ crucified. By the preaching of the law they are prepared to receive the grace of the Gospel.  <chapter eID="Ps.85"/> <div eID="gen21386" type="x-p"/>

entries.03fb9590225c985b86fd83f88c0d4a40c81da954: <div eID="gen9855" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Petition of the Hitherto Favoured People for a Restoration of Favour</title> <div sID="gen9856" type="x-p"/> The second part of the Book of Isaiah is written for the Israel of the Exile. It was the incidents of the Exile that first unsealed this great and indivisible prophecy, which in its compass is without any parallel. And after it had been unsealed there sprang up out of it those numerous songs of the Psalm-collection which remind us of their common model, partly by their allegorizing figurative language, partly by their lofty prophetic thoughts of consolation. This first Korahitic Jahve-Psalm (in <reference osisRef="Ps.85.13">Psa 85:13</reference> coming into contact with <reference osisRef="Ps.84.1-Ps.84.12">Psa 84:1-12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.84.12">Psa 84:12</reference>)), which more particularly by its allegorizing figurative language points to <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>, belongs to the number of these so-called deutero-Isaianic Psalms. The reference of <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.13">Psa 85:1-13</reference> to the period after the Exile and to the restoration of the state, says Dursch, is clearly expressed in the Psalm. On the other hand, Hengstenberg maintains that “the Psalm does not admit of any historical interpretation,” and is sure only of this one fact, that <reference osisRef="Ps.85.2-Ps.85.4">Psa 85:2-4</reference> do not relate to the deliverance out of the Exile. Even this Psalm, however, is not a formulary belonging to no express period, but has a special historical basis; and <reference osisRef="Ps.85.2-Ps.85.4">Psa 85:2-4</reference> certainly sound as though they came from the lips of a people restored to their fatherland.
entries.247c63be5e40a2c42a29a86a00b1f0ec5cd1e3a5: <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.3">Psa 85:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9857" type="x-p"/> The poet first of all looks back into the past, so rich in tokens of favour. The six perfects are a remembrance of former events, since nothing precedes to modify them. Certainly that which has just been experienced might also be intended; but then, as Hitzig supposes, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.5-Ps.85.8">Psa 85:5-8</reference> would be the petition that preceded it, and <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9">Psa 85:9</reference> would go back to the turning-point of the answering of the request - a retrograde movement which is less probable than that in shuwbeenuw, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.5">Psa 85:5</reference>, we have a transition to the petition for a renewal of previously manifested favour. (שׁבית) שבּ שׁבוּת, here said of a cessation of a national judgment, seems to be meant literally, not figuratively (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>). רצה, with the accusative, to have and to show pleasure in any one, as in the likewise Korahitic lamentation- <reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">Psa 44:4</reference>, cf. Psa 147:11. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.85.3">Psa 85:3</reference></hi> sin is conceived of as a burden of the conscience; in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.85.3">Psa 85:3</reference></hi> as a blood-stain. The music strikes up in the middle of the strophe in the sense of the “blessed” in Psa 32:1. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.85.4">Psa 85:4</reference></hi> God’s עברה (i.e., unrestrained wrath) appears as an emanation; He draws it back to Himself (אסף as in <reference osisRef="Joel.3.15">Joe 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.29">Psa 104:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19">1Sa 14:19</reference>) when He ceases to be angry; in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.85.4">Psa 85:4</reference></hi>, on the other hand, the fierce anger is conceived of as an active manifestation on the part of God which ceases when He turns round (השׁיב, <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. as inwardly transitive as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.6">Eze 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.25">Eze 39:25</reference>; cf. the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">Exo 32:12</reference>), i.e., gives the opposite turn to His manifestation.
entries.fd88dfa132b9c4250580900fd4778417de728d89: <reference osisRef="Ps.85.4-Ps.85.7">Psa 85:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen9857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9858" type="x-p"/> The poet now prays God to manifest anew the loving-kindness He has shown formerly. In the sense of “restore us again,” שׁוּבנוּ does not form any bond of connection between this and the preceding strophe; but it does it, according to Ges. §121, 4, it is intended in the sense of (אלינוּ) שׁוּב לנוּ, turn again to us. The poet prays that God would manifest Himself anew to His people as He has done in former days. Thus the transition from the retrospective perfects to the petition is, in the presence of the existing extremity, adequately brought about. Assuming the post-exilic origin of the Psalm, we see from this strophe that it was composed at a period in which the distance between the temporal and spiritual condition of Israel and the national restoration, promised together with the termination of the Exile, made itself distinctly felt. On עמּנוּ (in relation to and bearing towards us) beside כּעסך, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>, and also on הפר, Psa 89:34. In the question in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">Psa 89:6</reference> reminding God of His love and of His promise, משׁך has the signification of constant endless continuing or pursuing, as in Psa 36:11. The expression in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">Psa 85:7</reference></hi> is like <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">Psa 80:19</reference>; שׁוּב is here the representative of <hi type="italic">rursus</hi>, Ges. §142. ישׁעך from ישׁע, like קצפּך in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference>, has <hi type="italic">ĕ</hi> (cf. the inflexion of פּרי and חק) instead of the <hi type="italic">ı̆</hi> in אלהי ישׁענוּ. Here at the close of the strophe the prayer turns back inferentially to this attribute of God.
entries.41b2df2a79fad730bad3422ab4503e1b7287344f: <reference osisRef="Ps.85.8-Ps.85.10">Psa 85:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen9858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9859" type="x-p"/> The prayer is followed by attention to the divine answer, and by the answer itself. The poet stirs himself up to give ear to the words of God, like Habakkuk, Hab 2:1. Beside אשׁמעה we find the reading אשׁמעה, vid., on Psa 39:13. The construction of האל ה is appositional, like המּלך דּוד, Ges. §113. כּי neither introduces the divine answer in express words, nor states the ground on which he hearkens, but rather supports the fact that God speaks from that which He has to speak. Peace is the substance of that which He speaks to His people, and that (the particularizing <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>) to His saints; but with the addition of an admonition. אל is dehortative. It is not to be assumed in connection with this ethical notion that the <hi type="italic">ah</hi> of לכסלה is the locative <hi type="italic">ah</hi> as in לשׁאולה, Psa 9:18. כּסלה is related to כּסל like foolery to folly. The present misfortune, as is indicated here, is the merited consequence of foolish behaviour (playing the fool). In Psa 85:10. the poet unfolds the promise of peace which he has heard, just as he has heard it. What is meant by ישׁעו is particularized first by the infinitive, and then in perfects of actual fact. The possessions that make a people truly happy and prosperous are mentioned under a charming allegory exactly after Isaiah’s manner, Isa 32:16., <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>; Isa 59:14. The glory that has been far removed again takes up its abode in the land. Mercy or loving-kindness walks along the streets of Jerusalem, and there meets fidelity, like one guardian angel meeting the other. Righteousness and peace or prosperity, these two inseparable brothers, kiss each other there, and fall lovingly into each other’s arms.<note placement="foot">Concerning St. Bernard’s beautiful parable of the reconciliation of the inviolability of divine threatening and of justice with mercy and peace in the work of redemption, which has grown out of this passage of the Psalms, <hi type="italic">Misericordia et veritas obviaverunt sibi, justitia et pax osculatae sunt</hi>, and has been transferred to the painting, poetry, and drama of the middle ages, vid., Piper’s <hi type="italic">Evangelischer Kalender</hi>, 1859, S. 24-34, and the beautiful miniature representing the ἀσπασμός of δικαιοσύνη and εἰρήνη of a Greek Psalter, 1867, S. 63.</note>
entries.32bbb5c6a0747c676582850eba33b46e68a66933: <reference osisRef="Ps.85.11-Ps.85.13">Psa 85:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen9859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9860" type="x-p"/> The poet pursues this charming picture of the future further. After God’s אמת, i.e., faithfulness to the promises, has descended like dew, אמת, i.e., faithfulness to the covenant, springs up out of the land, the fruit of that fertilizing influence. And צדקה, gracious justice, looks down from heaven, smiling favour and dispensing blessing. גּם in <reference osisRef="Ps.85.13">Psa 85:13</reference> places these two prospects in reciprocal relation to one another (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.84.7">Psa 84:7</reference>); it is found once instead of twice. Jahve gives הטּוב, everything that is only and always good and that imparts true happiness, and the land, corresponding to it, yields יבוּלהּ, the increase which might be expected from a land so richly blessed (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.67.7">Psa 67:7</reference> and the promise in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4">Lev 26:4</reference>). Jahve Himself is present in the land: righteousness walks before Him majestically as His herald, and righteousness ישׂם לדרך פּעמיו, sets (viz., its footsteps) upon the way of His footsteps, that is to say, follows Him inseparably. פּעמיו stands once instead of twice; the construct is to a certain extent attractional, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.12">Psa 65:12</reference>; Gen 9:6. Since the expression is neither דּרך (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">Isa 51:10</reference>) nor לדּרך (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.11">Isa 49:11</reference>), it is natural to interpret the expression thus, and it gives moreover (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.58.8">Isa 58:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Isa 52:12</reference>) an excellent sense. But if, which we prefer, שׂים is taken in the sense of שׂים לב (as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>) with the following ל, to give special heed to anything (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.46">Deu 32:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.4">Eze 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.5">Eze 44:5</reference>), to be anxiously concerned about it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.20">1Sa 9:20</reference>), then we avoid the supplying in thought of a second פעמיו, which is always objectionable, and the thought obtained by the other interpretation is brought clearly before the mind: righteousness goes before Jahve, who dwells and walks abroad in Israel, and gives heed to the way of His steps, that is to say, follows carefully in His footsteps.  <chapter eID="Ps.85"/> <div eID="gen9860" type="x-p"/>

entries.e2f230381e304667c8f170a326badc402f543353:
PSALM 85
God having afflicted his people with new troubles and calamities, after their return from their captivity in Babylon, they, in the first place, make mention of their deliverance as an argument why he should not leave unfinished the work of his grace. Then they complain of the long continuance of their afflictions. And, in the third place, inspired with hope and confidence, they triumph in the blessedness promised them; for their restoration to their own country was connected with the kingdom of Christ, from which they anticipated an abundance of all good things.
“נשאת עון, nasata avon, ‘Thou hast borne, or carried away, the iniquity. An allusion to the ceremony of the scape-goat.” — Dr Adam Clarke “It is a maxim among the Jewish doctors,” says Hammond, “that captivity is one way of expiation, and so to return from thence was a sure indication that the sin for which it was inflicted was remitted or done away. This, saith Abarbanel, on Leviticus 16, was adumbrated in the Azazel, or scape-goat, which, as the other that was slain, was a sin-offering, as appears, Leviticus 16:5. ‘He shall take two kids for a sin-offering.’ And then the ‘confessing the sins over him,’ mentioned 16:21, (‘Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, etc., putting them on the head of the goat: And the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities into a land of separation,’ 16:22,) shows that they were to carry their sins with them into the land of their captivity, meant by the land of separation, that land whatsoever it was, whither the Divine Providence had designed their deportation. From whence therefore being now returned, their sins, for which they were thus punished, are supposed to be left behind them, no more to be laid to their charge, if their return to their former sins do not cause them to be called to remembrance.”
To the chief musician, a Psalm of the sons of Korah.
Psalm 85:1-4
1. O Jehovah! thou hast been favorable to thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. 2. Thou hast taken away the iniquity
“Ne faire qu’il ne fust enclin et pitie envers les enfans d’Abraham pour exaucer leurs prieres.” — Fr.
of thy people: thou hast covered all their sins. Selah. 3. Thou hast turned away all thy anger: thou hast drawn back the fury of thy indignation. 4. Turn us, O God of our salvation! and cause thy anger against us to cease.
 
1 O Jehovah! thou hast been favorable to thy land. Those who translate these words in the future tense, in my opinion, mar their meaning. This psalm, it is probable, was endited to be sung by the people when they were persecuted by the cruel tyranny of Antiochus; and from the deliverance wrought for them in the past, they were encouraged to expect in the future, fresh and continued tokens of the divine favor, — God having thereby testified, that their sins, however numerous and aggravated, could not efface from his memory the remembrance of his covenant, so as to render him inexorable towards the children of Abraham, and deaf to their prayers.
“Ou, si est ce que.” — Fr. marg. “Or, Yet.”
Had they not previously experienced such remarkable proofs of the divine goodness, they must necessarily have been overwhelmed with the load of their present afflictions, especially when so long protracted. The cause of their deliverance from captivity they attribute to the free love with which God had embraced the land which he had chosen for himself. Whence it follows, that the course of his favor was unintermitted; and the faithful also were inspired with confidence in prayer, by the reflection that, mindful of his choice, he had shown himself merciful to his own land. We have elsewhere had occasion to remark, that nothing contributes more effectually to encourage us to come to the throne of grace, than the remembrance of God’s former benefits. Our faith would immediately succumb under adversity, and sorrow would choke our hearts, were we not taught to believe from the experience of the past, that he is inclined compassionately to hear the prayers of his servants, and always affords them succor when the exigencies of their circumstances require it; especially as there remains at all times the same reason for continuing his goodness. Thus the prophet happily applies to believers of his own day, the benefits which God in old time bestowed upon their fathers, because both they and their fathers were called to the hope of the same inheritance.

                     <ns0:head>The ARGUMENT.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p>This <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> is thought to have been made after the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples return from the <ns0:hi>Babylonish</ns0:hi> Captivity: wherein he partly gives God thanks for that glorious deliver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance; and partly implores God's mercy in com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pleating that work, and rescuing his People from the Relicks of their Bondage, and from the vexa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion which they had by their Neighbours after they were returned to <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:head>To the chief musician. <ns0:hi>A Psalm</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> of.</ns0:note> for the sons of Korah.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 LORD, thou hast been <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> well plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed.</ns0:note> favourable unto thy land <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> unto thy People, in removing the sad effects of thy displeasure.</ns0:note>: thou hast brought back the captivity <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Captives, as that Word is used, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 14. 7. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 68. 18. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> of Jacob.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 32. 1:</ns0:note> Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lah <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">So as not-to impute it to them, or to continue the punishment which thou didst inflict upon them for it<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Thou hast taken away all thy wrath <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Those Calamities which were the effects of thy just wrath conceived against us.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> thou hast turned thine an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger from wax<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sag hot.</ns0:note> thou hast turned <ns0:hi>thy self</ns0:hi> from the fierceness of thine anger.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Turn us <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either 1. Convert us. As thou hast brought back our bodies to thy Land, so bring back our hearts to thy self, from whom many of them to this day are alienated. Or rather, 2. Restore us to our former tranquillity, and free us from the troubles which we yet groan under from our malicious Neighbours and Enemies. For this best suits with the following Clause of the Verse, which commonly explains the former.</ns0:note>, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger towards us to cease <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He prudent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly indeavours to take away the root and cause of their conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nued miseries, to wit, God's anger procured by their sins.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Wilt thou be angry with us for ever? wilt thou draw out thine anger to all genera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Wilt thou not revive us again <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Thou hast once revived us in bringing us out of Capti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vity, give us a second reviving in bringing home the rest of our Brethren, and in rebuking and restraining the Remainder of our Enemies wrath.</ns0:note>: that thy people may rejoyce in thee?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Shew us <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Grant it to us, as the next words explain it, and as <ns0:hi>shewing</ns0:hi> signifies, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 4. 6. So also <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. 3. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 71. 20. Or, manifest thy secret purpose of mercy to us by thy providen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tial Dispensations.</ns0:note> thy mercy, O LORD, and grant us thy salvation.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 I will hear <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Diligently observe: And the Psalmist by decla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring what he would do, teacheth all the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> what they ought to do. Or, he speaks in the name of all the People of God.</ns0:note> what God the LORD will speak <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either by his Prophets or Messengers: or by the works of his providence; for that also hath a voice. What Answer God will give to these my Prayers.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zech. 9. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> he will speak peace <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For I am assured from God's gracious nature and declared will and promise, that he will give an answer of peace.</ns0:note> unto his people, and to his saints <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which Clause seems to be added by way of explication and restriction, to shew that this glorious privilege did not belong to all that were called God's <ns0:hi>people,</ns0:hi> but onely to those that were truly and really such, even <ns0:hi>to his saints</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>holy ones.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: but let them not turn again to folly <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) To sin, which in Scripture is commonly called <ns0:hi>folly.</ns0:hi> This is added as a ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary caution, but when God shall speak peace to his People, let them not grow wanton and secure, nor return to their for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer wicked courses; which if they do, they will provoke God to repent of his kindness to them, and to inflict further and sorer judgments upon them. Others render the place, <ns0:hi>And they will not,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>That they may not return to folly.</ns0:hi> But the Par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticle <ns0:hi>al</ns0:hi> being prohibitive, our Translation seems to be better.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Surely his salvation <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That compleat salvation and deliverance for which all the <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> of God do pray and wait; even the Redemption of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> by the <ns0:hi>Messiah;</ns0:hi> of which not only Christian, but even Jewish Writers understand this place; and to which the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing passage do most properly and perfectly belong. And the Psalmist might well say of this Salvation that it was <ns0:hi>nigh,</ns0:hi> because the seventy weeks determined by <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> for this work, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9. 24. were now begun, this Psalm being written after <ns0:hi>Daniel's</ns0:hi> time.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> nigh them that fear him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The true <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> of God, even all those that love and fear him. By which words he both excludes all hypocritical <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> from this salvation, and tacitly assigns it to all that fear God, whether Jews or Gentiles.</ns0:note>: that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zech. 2. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> glory may dwell in our Land <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And when that Salvation shall come we shall be freed from all that scorn and contempt under which we now groan, and shall recover our ancient glory; and the glorious presence of God, the most eminent tokens whereof we have now utterly lost; and the God of Glory himself, even Christ, who is called <ns0:hi>the brightness of his</ns0:hi> Father's <ns0:hi>glory,</ns0:hi> Heb. 1. 3. comp. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1. 14. and <ns0:hi>the glory of Israel,</ns0:hi> Luk. 2. 32. shall come and visibly dwell in this now despised Land.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Mercy and truth are met together: righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness and peace <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This is to be understood, either 1. Of these Graces or Vertues in men. So the sence is, when that blessed time shall come, those Virtues which now seem to be banished from hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mane Societies, shall be restored, and there shall be an happy conjunction of <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> or benignity; <ns0:hi>truth</ns0:hi> or veracity; <ns0:hi>righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness</ns0:hi> or faithfulness; and <ns0:hi>peace</ns0:hi> or peaceableness and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cord. Or rather 2. Of the Blessings of God, of which the whole Context speaks. And the sence is, That great Work of Redemption by Christ shall clearly manifest and demonstrate God's <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> in redeeming his People of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and in the call<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing and conversion of the Gentiles; his <ns0:hi>truth</ns0:hi> in fulfilling that great promise of the sending of his Son, which is the Foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dation of all the rest; his <ns0:hi>righteousness</ns0:hi> in punishing sin, or un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />righteousness in his Son, and in conferring righteousness upon guilty and lost creatures; and his <ns0:hi>peace</ns0:hi> or reconciliation to sinners, and that peace of conscience which attends upon it<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> kave kissed <ns0:hi>each other</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">As Friends use to do when they meet<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 4. 27. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 18. 7. So this is another expression of the same thing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Truth shall spring out of the earth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either 1. Truth among men, which shall be so com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon amongst all men, as if it grew out of the earth. Or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 2. The truth or faithfulness of God; which is most tru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly and fitly said to <ns0:hi>spring out of the earth,</ns0:hi> partly because it had long been hid and buried like a <ns0:hi>root in a dry ground,</ns0:hi> with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out any hopes of a reviving; from whence yet God made it to grow, as is noted, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53. 2. and partly because Christ, who is <ns0:hi>the truth, Iohn</ns0:hi> 14. 6. and <ns0:hi>a minister of the circumcision, (i. e.</ns0:hi> of the circumcised, or of the Jews) <ns0:hi>for the truth of God to confirm the promises made unto the fathers,</ns0:hi> was born upon the earth of a Virgin's Womb.</ns0:note>: and righteousness shall look down from heaven <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Even God's Justice, which was offended with men, shall then be satisfied, and shall through Christ look down upon sinful men with a reconciled and smiling countenance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:482" />12 Yea, the LORD shall give <ns0:hi>that which is</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) All that is good in it self and for us, all spiritu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al and temporal Blessings.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Pal. 67. 6.</ns0:note> our land shall yield her in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crease.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 89. 14.</ns0:note> Righteousness shall go before him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">As his Harbenger or Attendant. He shall work and full<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fill all righteousness, he shall glorifie and satisfie the righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of God, and shall advance the practice of righteousness and holiness among men.</ns0:note>: and shall set <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>hir steps i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>e way,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> steps in t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>e way. So Gr.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>us</ns0:hi> in the way of his steps <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) shall cause us to walk in those righteous ways wherein he walketh, and which he hath prescribed to us. But this <ns0:hi>us</ns0:hi> is not in the Hebrew, and may seem too liberal a supplement. And the words may be, and are by almost all other Interpreters, rendred otherwise, <ns0:hi>He (i. e.</ns0:hi> God) <ns0:hi>shall set</ns0:hi> (which may note his stability and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stancy in so doing) it (to wit, <ns0:hi>righteousness</ns0:hi> last mentioned) <ns0:hi>in the way of his steps, (i. e.</ns0:hi>) in the way wherein he walketh. So the sence of this last Clause is the same for substance with the former, as is very usual in this Book; righteousness in that Clause goes before him, and in this it goes along with him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
